claim: Bioelectric currents and potentials in the body (EEG band included) can be treated in the quasistatic limit of Maxwell's equations: at every instant all currents and fields behave as if stationary, and all volume conductors are assumed linear.

source.authors: Malmivuo J, Plonsey R
source.title: Bioelectromagnetism: Principles and Applications of Bioelectric and Biomagnetic Fields (Chapter 7, Volume Source and Volume Conductor)

evidence_location: Chapter 7, Section 7.2.4 'Quasistatic Conditions' (and Sec. 7.2.2 statement that all volume conductors are assumed linear)
quote: can be examined in the conventional quasistatic limit (Plonsey and Heppner, 1967)
notes: Opened via plain HTTP curl of bem.fi (WebFetch loops on the http/https redirect). Same chapter: 'all volume conductors are assumed to be linear (consistent with all experimental evidence)'. Hamalainen et al. 1993 Sec. III.A pp. 426-427 says the same ('we can adopt the quasistatic approximation').

claim: Extracellular potentials from multiple current sinks and sources combine linearly by the superposition principle, so every current in the brain adds at a given point to yield the local extracellular voltage.

source.authors: Buzsaki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents - EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Section 'The role of volume conduction in Ve' (author manuscript, PMC4907333)
quote: Multiple current sinks and sources then combine linearly by the superposition principle.
notes: Also, 'Contributors to extracellular fields': 'All currents in the brain superimpose at any given point in space to yield Ve at that location.' DOI not displayed on the fetched page; taken from standard citation.

claim: The two most important determinants of extracellular field strength are the spatial alignment of neurons and the temporal synchrony of their current sources; measurable signals require currents from many compartments to overlap in time.

source.authors: Buzsaki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents - EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Sections 'Neuronal geometry and architecture' and 'Synaptic activity'
quote: the two most important determinants of the extracellular field strength are the spatial alignment of neurons
notes: Also: 'extracellular currents from many individual compartments must overlap in time to induce a measurable signal'. The review does NOT state an explicit N vs sqrt(N) rule; see t2-04 for that.

claim: In a population model of the LFP, uncorrelated (asynchronous) single-cell contributions add in variance (power ~ N, amplitude ~ sqrt N), whereas fully correlated (synchronous) contributions add in amplitude (amplitude ~ N); with correlated input the population signal stops saturating with population size.

source.authors: Leski S, Linden H, Tetzlaff T, Pettersen KH, Einevoll GT
source.title: Frequency dependence of signal power and spatial reach of the local field potential

evidence_location: Section 2.2 (Eqs. 3-4) and Section 2.4 of the arXiv/ar5iv version (1302.4559); PMC3715549 is the journal version
quote: In the case of uncorrelated input this amounts to simply adding the variances of the single-cell LFPs.
notes: For correlated input the text says the signal is found by 'adding the single amplitudes, not variances', and in Sec. 2.4 'the power of the population signal no longer seems to saturate as the population radius increases'. The sqrt(N)/N exponents are the direct mathematical consequence of these two statements, not written explicitly in the paper. Verified in the arXiv version, not the PLoS page.

claim: For uncorrelated synaptic activity the LFP represents cells within a radius of only a few hundred micrometres, but when contributions from different cells are correlated the generating region grows to the spatial extent of the correlated activity.

source.authors: Linden H, Tetzlaff T, Potjans TC, Pettersen KH, Grun S, Diesmann M, Einevoll GT
source.title: Modeling the spatial reach of the LFP

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 22153380)
quote: For uncorrelated activity, the LFP represents cells in a small region (within a radius of a few hundred micrometers).
notes: Abstract only (full text not opened). Next sentence: 'If the LFP contributions from different cells are correlated, the size of the generating region is determined by the spatial extent of the correlated activity.'

claim: A typical equivalent current dipole measured with MEG/EEG, produced by the synchronous activity of probably tens of thousands of neurons, has a strength of about 10 nA·m.

source.authors: Hamalainen M, Hari R, Ilmoniemi RJ, Knuutila J, Lounasmaa OV
source.title: Magnetoencephalography - theory, instrumentation, and applications to noninvasive studies of the working human brain

evidence_location: Section I.C, p. 417
quote: caused by the synchronous activity of probably tens of thousands of neurons, is 10 nA m.
notes: Separate nA·m values for alpha rhythm or epileptic spikes are NOT given in this paper; Sec. I.E gives only magnetic field amplitudes (alpha 1-2 pT; evoked responses tens to hundreds of fT; epileptic spikes 'even larger amplitude').

claim: A single postsynaptic potential produces a current dipole of only ~20 fA·m, so roughly a million synapses must be simultaneously active to yield the ~10 nA·m dipole seen in a typical evoked response.

source.authors: Hamalainen M, Hari R, Ilmoniemi RJ, Knuutila J, Lounasmaa OV
source.title: Magnetoencephalography - theory, instrumentation, and applications to noninvasive studies of the working human brain

evidence_location: Section II.D, p. 424
quote: we find that Q= 20 fA m for a single PSP
notes: Derived in the paper from dendrite diameter 1 um, intracellular conductivity 0.1 S/m, and 25 mV PSP. Same page: dipole moments needed to explain external fields 'are on the order of 10 nAm', implying 'about a million synapses must be simultaneously active during a typical evoked response'.

claim: Given ~10^5 pyramidal cells per mm² of cortex and thousands of synapses per neuron, activating as few as one synapse in a thousand over 1 mm² would produce a detectable MEG/EEG signal; a 10 nA·m dipole corresponds to roughly 40 mm² of active cortex.
units: mm² of active cortex per 10 nA·m

source.authors: Hamalainen M, Hari R, Ilmoniemi RJ, Knuutila J, Lounasmaa OV
source.title: Magnetoencephalography - theory, instrumentation, and applications to noninvasive studies of the working human brain

evidence_location: Section II.D, pp. 424-425
quote: a dipole moment of 10 nAm would correspond to 40 mm of active cortex
notes: PDF text extraction dropped superscripts: the source reads '40 mm' and '10 pyramidal cells per mm'; physically these are 40 mm² and 10^5 cells per mm² (consistent with Rockel-derived densities, t2-15). Also quoted: 'the simultaneous activation of as few as one synapse in a thousand over an area of one square millimeter would suffice to produce a detectable signal'.

claim: In compartmental models of real neocortical neurons, a single layer V pyramidal cell produces a current dipole of about 0.4-0.9 pA·m during the slow depolarization envelope of a burst (spikes -0.78 to +2.97 pA·m), and a layer II/III pyramidal cell about 0.29 pA·m (envelope) and 0.47 pA·m (spike).
units: pA·m per layer V pyramidal cell (envelope, max)

source.authors: Murakami S, Okada Y
source.title: Contributions of principal neocortical neurons to magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 16613883; full text PMC1995687 was CAPTCHA-blocked)
quote: The envelope was similar in magnitude (-0.41 to -0.90 pA m) across the four layer V pyramidal cells.
notes: Also in abstract: 'The spikes produced by the layer V pyramidal cells (n = 4) varied between -0.78 and 2.97 pA m'; 'The spike and envelope for the layer II/III pyramidal cell were 0.47 and -0.29 pA m'. Guinea-pig-derived morphologies; sign = direction (positive toward pia).

claim: Stellate cells produce much weaker dipoles than pyramidal cells (layer IV spiny stellate 0.27 pA·m, layer III aspiny stellate 0.06 pA·m along their best orientation), and a population of stellate cells sums to less than the linear sum of individual dipoles because of their variable dendritic geometry.

source.authors: Murakami S, Okada Y
source.title: Contributions of principal neocortical neurons to magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 16613883)
quote: stronger for the layer IV spiny stellate (0.27 pA m) than the layer III aspiny stellate cell (0.06 pA m)
notes: Abstract also: 'The Q for a population of stellate cells may be weaker than a linear sum of their individual Q values due to their variable dendritic geometry' - i.e., the closed-field cancellation argument. 'The stellate cells lacked the envelope.'

claim: Burst discharges of neocortical pyramidal cells may become detectable with MEG and EEG when about 10,000-50,000 cells are synchronously active.

source.authors: Murakami S, Okada Y
source.title: Contributions of principal neocortical neurons to magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals

evidence_location: Abstract, final sentence (Europe PMC record, PMID 16613883)
quote: may be detectable with MEG and EEG when 10 000-50 000 cells are synchronously active
notes: Consistent with 10 nA·m / (0.2-1 pA·m per cell). The abstract does not state the ~10 nA·m detection threshold explicitly; that number comes from Hamalainen 1993 (t2-06).

claim: Synaptic (postsynaptic) currents are usually the most important source of extracellular current flow because they are slow enough to overlap in time, whereas the strongest action-potential fields last under 2 ms and nearby neurons rarely fire synchronously within such short windows.

source.authors: Buzsaki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents - EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Sections 'Synaptic activity' and 'Fast action potentials'
quote: nearby neurons rarely fire synchronously in such short time windows under physiological conditions
notes: Also: 'In physiological situations, synaptic activity is often the most important source of extracellular current flow'; 'such overlap is most easily achieved for relatively slow events, such as synaptic currents'; 'the strongest fields they generate are of short duration (<2 ms)'.

claim: EEG and MEG are produced largely by approximately dipolar synaptic current flow lasting tens of milliseconds; the ~1 ms action potential instead forms two opposed dipoles (a current quadrupole) that contributes little at a distance.
units: ms (action potential duration) vs tens of ms (synaptic currents)

source.authors: Hamalainen M, Hari R, Ilmoniemi RJ, Knuutila J, Lounasmaa OV
source.title: Magnetoencephalography - theory, instrumentation, and applications to noninvasive studies of the working human brain

evidence_location: Section II.E, p. 425
quote: EEG and MEG signals are produced in large part by synaptic current flow, which is approximately dipolar.
notes: Same page: synaptic currents 'last tens of milliseconds' while action potentials 'have a duration of 1 ms only'; 'Since the two dipoles are opposite, they form a current quadrupole.'

claim: Pyramidal cells, the most populous cortical cell type, have long thick apical dendrites that generate strong dipoles along the somatodendritic axis (open field), whereas spherically symmetric neurons with dendrites of equal size (e.g., thalamocortical cells) tend toward closed fields that cancel at a distance when several dendrites are activated together.

source.authors: Buzsaki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents - EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Section 'Neuronal geometry and architecture'
quote: They have long, thick apical dendrites that can generate strong dipoles along the somatodendritic axis.
notes: Also: 'Pyramidal cells are the most populous cell type'; 'spherically symmetric neurons - such as thalamocortical cells - that emanate dendrites of relatively equal size'; 'a strictly closed field only occurs when several dendrites are simultaneously activated'. Lorente de No (1947) is NOT cited by name in this review.

claim: Large deep-layer cortical pyramidal neurons, with apical dendrites oriented perpendicular to the cortical surface, play the major role in generating the EEG; electrotonic spread of excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials along those dendrites turns them into electrical dipoles.

source.authors: Kirschstein T, Kohling R
source.title: What is the source of the EEG?

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 19715175)
quote: large cortical pyramidal neurons in deep cortical layers play a major role in the generation of the EEG
notes: Abstract also: 'By electrotonic spread of postsynaptic potentials along the apical dendrites and equivalent capacitive currents, they become electrical dipoles', and both excitatory and inhibitory inputs produce deflections depending on synapse location. Full text (SAGE) not opened.

claim: Rockel, Hiorns & Powell (1980) counted ~110 neurons in a 30-µm-wide strip (750 µm²) through the full cortical depth, equivalent to ~147,000 neurons under 1 mm² of cortical surface, in motor, somatosensory, frontal, parietal and temporal cortex of mouse, rat, cat, monkey and man (binocular primate area 17 ~2.5x more).
units: neurons per mm² of cortical surface (full depth)

source.authors: Rockel AJ, Hiorns RW, Powell TP
source.title: The basic uniformity in structure of the neocortex

evidence_location: Rockel 1980 abstract (Europe PMC, PMID 6772266) for the ~110-per-30-um-strip count; the per-mm² conversion (147,000) is stated in the abstract of Herculano-Houzel et al. 2008 PNAS 105:12593, doi 10.1073/pnas.0805417105 (PMC2527956)
quote: the same absolute number (congruent to 110) of neurons has been found in all areas and in all species
notes: Herculano-Houzel 2008 abstract: 'approximately 110 neurons underneath a surface area of 750 microm(2) (147,000 underneath 1 mm(2))', but that study found the number under 1 mm² 'is not constant and varies by three times across' nine primate species. Full-depth counts; the oft-quoted '~10^5 per mm²' is this figure rounded.

claim: A 2013 replication with modern stereology confirmed Rockel et al.: the number of neurons under a square millimetre of cortical surface is the same across five cortical areas and five species despite differing cortical thickness.

source.authors: Carlo CN, Stevens CF
source.title: Structural uniformity of neocortex, revisited
source.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 23297199 / PMC3557031; full text CAPTCHA-blocked on PMC)
quote: We have replicated these experiments and confirm the accuracy of the original report.
notes: The abstract does not restate the absolute count; see t2-16 for the number. Abstract also notes glial number under 1 mm² depends on cortical thickness.

claim: Approximately one in five neocortical neurons is GABAergic (inhibitory) in many areas and species, so roughly 80% are excitatory neurons, of which pyramidal cells are the main class.
units: fraction of neocortical neurons that are GABAergic

source.authors: Sahara S, Yanagawa Y, O'Leary DD, Stevens CF
source.title: The fraction of cortical GABAergic neurons is constant from near the start of cortical neurogenesis to adulthood

evidence_location: Abstract, first sentence (Europe PMC record, PMID 22492031)
quote: Approximately one in five neurons is GABAergic in many neocortical areas and species
notes: Replaces DeFelipe & Farinas 1992 (its Europe PMC record has no abstract text, so the 70-85% pyramidal figure could not be verified). The '80% excitatory = mostly pyramidal' inference is mine; spiny stellate cells (layer IV) are also excitatory.

claim: Glial cells can contribute to extracellular potentials, but the glial syncytium is thought to contribute only to slow and infraslow (<0.1 Hz) field patterns, i.e., below the conventional EEG band.
units: Hz (upper bound of glia-attributed infraslow activity)

source.authors: Buzsaki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents - EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Section 'Gap junctions and neuron-glia interactions'
quote: the glial syncytium may contribute to slow and infraslow (<0.1 Hz) field patterns
notes: Hedged ('may') in source. Also: 'Membrane potential changes in non-neuronal cells, such as glia, may also give rise to Ve'; 'These slow LFPs may arise from glia, glia-neuron interactions or from vascular events'. The review does not discuss spreading depression or K+ buffering; no primary glial DC-potential measurement (Somjen 1973) was opened.

claim: Dendritic Ca2+ spikes are large (10-50 mV) and long-lasting, so their share of measured extracellular events can be substantial under certain circumstances; they are often triggered by NMDA-receptor-mediated EPSPs, and inhibitory (often hyperpolarizing) synaptic currents can also generate substantial transmembrane currents.

source.authors: Buzsaki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents - EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Sections 'Calcium spikes' and 'Synaptic activity'
quote: Because dendritic Ca2+ spikes are large (10-50 mV) and long lasting
notes: Continues: 'their share in the measured extracellular events can be substantial under certain circumstances'; 'regenerative Ca2+ spikes are often triggered by NMDA receptor-mediated excitatory postsynaptic potentials'; 'inhibitory (and often hyperpolarizing) currents can generate substantial transmembrane currents'. Larkum 1999 not opened.

claim: Spike-triggered unitary LFPs in human temporal cortex (layer II/III, Utah array, 140 neurons) and monkey premotor cortex (150 neurons) indicate that the LFP reflects primarily inhibitory (fast-spiking) neuron activity; whitened unitary LFPs reach no further than ~1 mm from the trigger neuron (space constants 0.15-0.25 mm).
units: mm (maximum reach of whitened unitary LFP)

source.authors: Telenczuk B, Dehghani N, Le Van Quyen M, Cash SS, Halgren E, Hatsopoulos NG, Destexhe A
source.title: Local field potentials primarily reflect inhibitory neuron activity in human and monkey cortex

evidence_location: Abstract (final sentence); Results pp. 2-3 and Fig. 1E / Fig. 3 for space constants
quote: in human and monkey neocortex, the LFP reflects primarily inhibitory neuron activity
notes: Range field = whitened space constants (RS 0.20-0.25 mm, FS 0.15-0.20 mm). Caution: amplitudes of inhibitory vs excitatory unitary LFPs did NOT differ significantly at 0.4-2 mm in most recordings; the 'primarily inhibitory' conclusion rests on latency/propagation and the proposal that excitatory unitary LFPs arise di-synaptically via interneurons. No microvolt ratio is given.

claim: EEG sensitivity depends only weakly on source orientation (median ratio of weakest-to-strongest orientation 0.63, 95% above 0.42) whereas MEG is nearly blind to one orientation at most cortical locations (median 0.06, 95% below 0.23) and insensitive to radial sources.
units: ratio of minimum to maximum orientation sensitivity (EEG)

source.authors: Ahlfors SP, Han J, Belliveau JW, Hamalainen MS
source.title: Sensitivity of MEG and EEG to source orientation

evidence_location: Abstract; Results para. 1 and Fig. 1; Discussion para. 1-2
quote: was 0.06 for MEG and 0.63 for EEG
notes: Results: 'For MEG, the median value of R lambda was 0.06 and 95% of the values were below 0.23'; EEG '95% of the values were above 0.42'. Discussion: for MEG, depth rather than orientation is 'likely to be the critical factor'. No quantitative EEG depth-attenuation curve in this paper. DOI not shown on fetched page.

claim: In simultaneous scalp and intracranial recordings from 16 temporal-lobe-epilepsy patients, intracranial interictal spikes involving <6 cm² of cortex were never seen on scalp EEG, only 10% of spikes with <10 cm² produced scalp spikes, and 90% of spikes with >10 cm² did; synchronous activation of 10-20 cm² of gyral cortex was common.

source.authors: Tao JX, Ray A, Hawes-Ebersole S, Ebersole JS
source.title: Intracranial EEG substrates of scalp EEG interictal spikes

evidence_location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (Europe PMC record, PMID 15857432)
quote: Intracranial spikes with <6 cm(2) of area were never associated with scalp EEG spikes.
notes: Also: '90% of cortical spikes with a source area of >10 cm(2) produced scalp EEG spikes, whereas only 10% of cortical spikes having <10 cm(2) of source area produced scalp potentials'; 'Synchronous or at least temporally overlapping activation of 10-20 cm(2) of gyral cortex is common.' Primary modern measurement that supersedes the Cooper 1965 '6 cm²' figure (t2-25).

claim: Scalp EEG is a spatiotemporally smoothed version of the LFP integrated over a cortical area of 10 cm² or more.
units: cm² (minimum cortical area integrated by a scalp EEG electrode)

source.authors: Buzsaki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents - EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Box 1, 'Electroencephalography'
quote: integrated over an area of 10 cm2 or more
notes: Box 1 also states ECoG spatial resolution 'can be substantially improved (<5 mm2)'. Consistent with Tao 2005 (t2-23).

claim: Cooper et al. (1965) is the classic source for the statement that roughly 6 cm² of synchronously active cortex is needed for activity to be visible on the scalp, based on simultaneous chronic subcortical, cortical and scalp recordings in man.

source.authors: Cooper R, Winter AL, Crow HJ, Walter WG
source.title: Comparison of subcortical, cortical and scalp activity using chronically indwelling electrodes in man

evidence_location: Could not be verified: Europe PMC (PMID 14255050) and scilit show 'No abstract available'; full text paywalled (Elsevier)
notes: Only the bibliographic record (title, journal, volume, pages, DOI) was seen. The 6 cm² figure is widely attributed to this paper (e.g., via Nunez) but was not seen in the source. Use Tao 2005 (t2-23: <6 cm² never visible; >10 cm² usually visible) as the citable primary measurement instead.
